why.correct: Membrane potential is always read as the inside compared with the outside. A negative value means the inside face of the membrane carries a slight excess of negative charge relative to the outside face.
options: Correct. By convention the value is the inside relative to the outside, so −70 mV means the inside is 70 mV more negative.
This reverses the convention. The outside is the reference, and it is the inside that is negative.
Millivolts measure voltage, not concentration. Building −70 mV takes far fewer ions than that, and concentrations barely change.
The bulk cytosol is electrically neutral. The extra negative charge sits in a thin layer right against the inner face of the membrane.

why.correct: With only potassium able to cross, potassium leaves until the electrical pull inward balances its concentration push outward. That balance point is potassium's equilibrium potential, about −90 mV with these concentrations.
options: Potassium still leaks out and leaves negative charge behind, so a voltage builds. A membrane passing only potassium settles at potassium's equilibrium potential, not at zero.
Real cells rest near −70 mV because a small sodium leak pulls them up from potassium's value. With no sodium leak, nothing pulls the voltage away from −90 mV.
About +60 mV is sodium's equilibrium potential. It would apply to a membrane that passed only sodium.
Correct. A membrane permeable only to potassium reaches potassium's equilibrium potential, about −90 mV.

why.correct: The membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane passes most easily. At rest, many potassium leak channels are open and few pass sodium, so the voltage sits near potassium's −90 mV, pulled only slightly toward sodium's +60 mV.
options: Potassium ions are actually heavier than sodium ions, not lighter, and ion size does not set the resting value anyway. What matters is how many open channels each ion has.
Correct. Permeability decides which ion dominates, and at rest the membrane passes potassium tens of times more easily than sodium.
The pump moves 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in, so it moves more sodium, not more potassium. Its direct effect on the voltage is only a few millivolts anyway.
Most of the body's sodium is outside cells and most potassium inside; total amounts do not decide the voltage. The open channels do.

why.correct: Raising outside potassium shrinks the potassium concentration gradient. Less potassium needs to leave before the electrical pull balances it, so potassium's equilibrium potential moves toward zero, and the resting potential follows. The cells are depolarized.
options: The voltage comes from potassium leaving the cell, not from potassium sitting outside. A smaller gradient means less leaves, so the inside becomes less negative, not more.
The inside concentration barely changes, but the gradient depends on both sides. Outside potassium rising from about 4 to 7 mmol/L is a large relative change and shrinks the gradient.
Correct. Hyperkalemia depolarizes resting cells by shrinking the potassium gradient that drives the leak.
Potassium still dominates at rest, and its equilibrium potential with 7 mmol/L outside is still well below zero (around −80 mV). The cell depolarizes but stays negative.

why.correct: Hypokalemia (low blood potassium) makes the potassium gradient larger. More potassium must leave before the electrical pull balances it, so potassium's equilibrium potential and the resting potential both become more negative: the cells hyperpolarize.
options: Correct. Low outside potassium steepens the gradient, and in most cells the resting potential hyperpolarizes.
Less negative is the effect of high blood potassium, which shrinks the gradient.
The resting potential stays negative. Potassium still dominates, and its equilibrium potential moves further below zero, not above it.
Outside potassium helps set the gradient that drives the leak. A drop from about 4 to 2.8 mmol/L is a large relative change, so the voltage shifts.

why.correct: Potassium leaving carries positive charge out, and the trapped negative proteins it leaves behind cannot follow. The pump adds a small extra negativity because it exports one more positive charge than it imports each cycle.
options: Correct. This is the main source of the resting potential.
Correct. These trapped anions are the negative charge left unbalanced when potassium leaves.
Correct, but small. Its direct contribution is only a few millivolts.
Sodium entering brings positive charge in. It pulls the voltage toward sodium's +60 mV, making the inside less negative.
Water carries no net charge, so osmosis does not directly change the membrane potential.

why.correct: Depolarization is any change that makes the potential less negative than rest. It does not have to reach zero or become positive.
options: Hyperpolarization is a change to more negative than rest, such as −70 to −80 mV.
Repolarization is a return toward rest after a depolarization. This change moves away from rest.
Correct. Moving from −70 to −60 mV is a depolarization, even though the inside stays negative.
Reversal of polarity would mean the inside became positive. Here it is still negative; it has only moved toward zero, which is a depolarization.

why.correct: More open potassium channels let more potassium leave, so the voltage moves further toward potassium's equilibrium potential. A value more negative than rest is a hyperpolarization.
options: Potassium flows out of the cell, down its concentration gradient, not in. Potassium entering would make the inside less negative.
Correct. Increasing potassium permeability pulls the membrane toward potassium's −90 mV, a hyperpolarization.
A sodium leak would move the voltage toward sodium's +60 mV, a depolarization. The voltage here became more negative.
Exporting fewer positive ions would make the inside slightly less negative, the opposite of what happened. The cell also opened potassium channels, which is the direct cause.

why.correct: Repolarization (re- = again) is the return of the membrane potential toward its resting value after a depolarization.
options: Hyperpolarization would take the potential below −70 mV. This change stops at rest.
Depolarization is the move away from rest toward zero, which already happened on the way to +20 mV.
An equilibrium potential belongs to a single ion. The resting potential is a balance of several ions, and the return to it has its own name.
Correct. Moving from +20 mV back to −70 mV is repolarization.

why.correct: Raising outside potassium shrinks the potassium gradient, which makes potassium's equilibrium potential and the resting potential less negative, while inside concentration barely changes.

variables.name: Potassium concentration gradient across the membrane
variables.why: Outside potassium rises while inside stays near 140 mmol/L, so the difference between the two sides shrinks.

variables.name: How negative potassium's equilibrium potential is
variables.why: A smaller gradient is balanced by a smaller electrical pull, so potassium's equilibrium potential moves from about −95 toward −76 mV.

variables.name: How negative the resting membrane potential is
variables.why: Rest sits near potassium's equilibrium potential, so it follows it toward zero: the cell depolarizes.

variables.name: Potassium concentration inside the cell
variables.why: Only a tiny number of ions move to change the voltage, so the inside concentration stays near 140 mmol/L.

why.correct: Blocking the pump changes the voltage only a little at first, because leak channels, not the pump, make most of it. Over hours the gradients run down and the resting potential fades.

variables.name: How negative the resting potential is, in the first few seconds
variables.why: The pump's direct contribution disappears, but it was only a few millivolts, so the inside becomes only slightly less negative.

variables.name: Sodium concentration inside the cell, after several hours
variables.why: Sodium keeps leaking in and nothing pumps it back out, so it slowly accumulates.

variables.name: Potassium concentration gradient, after several hours
variables.why: Potassium keeps leaking out and is not replaced, so the gradient that drives the leak runs down.

variables.name: How negative the resting potential is, after several hours
variables.why: With the gradients fading, potassium leak can no longer hold the inside negative, and the voltage drifts toward zero.

why.correct: The gradients come first. Potassium then leaks out, leaving negative charge behind. That charge opposes further exit until the voltage nears −90 mV, and a small sodium leak pulls it up to about −70 mV.
Sodium is concentrated outside the cell, so it leaks in, not out. Its small inward leak makes the inside a little less negative.
options: This is right: potassium is concentrated inside the cell.
This is right: open potassium leak channels are the main route for charge at rest.
This is the error. Sodium diffuses into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, adding positive charge inside.
This is right: the electrical pull on potassium grows as the inside becomes more negative.
This is right for a typical neuron: between potassium's −90 mV and sodium's +60 mV, close to potassium's.

why.correct: The inside becomes negative only because the charge that potassium was balancing stays behind. Large negative proteins cannot cross the membrane.
options: Correct. Unbalanced negative charge left behind is what turns potassium loss into a voltage.
Sodium entering would add positive charge and oppose the negativity. At rest only a little sodium leaks in.
If the pump matched the leak instantly, no charge would separate on this timescale. The voltage comes from the leak itself.
If chloride left with potassium, the charges would cancel and no voltage would build.

why.correct: Very little charge has to cross a thin membrane to create tens of millivolts. The concentrations inside and outside barely change; only a thin film of charge builds on each face of the membrane.
options: If half the potassium left, the gradient itself would collapse. The number that moves is tiny.
The pump works steadily against the slow leak over time. It does not need to refill the cell after each voltage change, because each change moves very few ions.
Potassium does move at rest: its outward leak is what creates the voltage. The amount is just very small.
Correct. A tiny fraction of the potassium moves, and the concentrations stay essentially the same.

why.correct: The membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane passes most easily. With sodium dominating, the voltage heads toward sodium's equilibrium potential, about +60 mV.
options: About −90 mV is potassium's equilibrium potential. It applies when potassium dominates.
Correct. Sodium flows in, carrying positive charge, and the inside heads toward sodium's +60 mV.
Zero has no special pull. Sodium keeps flowing in past zero because its concentration gradient still pushes it inward.
The resting value depends on which channels are open. Changing the dominant ion changes the voltage.

why.correct: The pump's main job is long-term: it replaces the potassium that leaks out and removes the sodium that leaks in, keeping the gradients steady. Its direct voltage effect is only a few millivolts.
options: The pump's direct contribution is a few millivolts. Potassium leak makes most of the resting potential.
Correct. The pump maintains the gradients that the leak channels use.
The pump is a transporter, not a channel opener. Leak channels are open on their own.
The pump moves sodium out of the cell, against its gradient.

why.correct: The voltage between the two faces is still 70 mV. Measured from the inside, the outside is 70 mV more positive, so the meter reads +70 mV. That is why the convention always reports the inside relative to the outside.
options: This is the reading with the electrodes in their proper places. Swapping them flips the sign.
The charge separation has not changed, so the meter still sees a 70 mV difference.
Correct. Same size, opposite sign, because the reference point moved.
Swapping electrodes flips the sign; it does not double the size.

why.correct: Neurons make most of their ATP with oxygen. Without ATP the pumps slow, leaks continue, and the gradients that the leak channels depend on fade, so the resting potential fades too.
options: The leak channels do not need oxygen to stay in their usual state. The problem is the energy supply for the pump.
Correct. Energy failure stops the pump, and without the pump the gradients run down.
Potassium leak channels are passive; they do not need ATP to stay open.
Potassium keeps leaking out and is not pumped back, so inside potassium falls, not rises.

why.correct: Excitable cells are cells whose membranes can produce action potentials. Neurons and muscle fibers have the voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels this requires.
options: Correct. Neurons produce action potentials along their axons.
Correct. A skeletal muscle fiber's action potential starts its contraction.
Correct. Heart muscle cells produce action potentials, a longer kind covered in the heart chapter.
A red blood cell has a resting potential but lacks the voltage-gated channels needed for an action potential.
A fibroblast has a resting potential too, but it is not excitable.

why.correct: A graded potential is a small, local change whose size depends on stimulus strength. A stronger touch opens more mechanically gated channels, so the depolarization is larger.
options: Action potentials are all-or-none: they do not come in different sizes, and they start only at threshold, which neither touch reached.
Correct. Size tracking stimulus strength is the defining feature of a graded potential.
A refractory period is a time after an action potential when the membrane cannot fire again. No action potential happened here.
Hyperpolarization makes the membrane more negative. These changes made it less negative.

why.correct: Below threshold, the few sodium channels that open cannot outpace potassium leaving, so the self-reinforcing cycle never starts. The graded potential fades and the membrane returns to about −70 mV.
options: There is no small action potential. Action potentials are all-or-none.
No action potential occurs at all if threshold is not reached, delayed or otherwise.
Correct. A subthreshold depolarization is a graded potential that dies away.
Graded potentials are short-lived. Potassium leak pulls the membrane back to rest once the stimulus ends.

why.correct: Action potentials are all-or-none, so their size does not change. A stronger stimulus makes a larger graded potential at the nerve ending, which triggers action potentials more often. Frequency carries the strength.
options: The peak is set by the sodium and potassium channels, not by the stimulus. Every action potential in this fiber reaches about the same peak.
Duration is also set by the channels' timing, so each action potential lasts about the same time.
Correct. Stimulus strength is coded as how many action potentials arrive per second.
Speed depends on the axon itself, such as its diameter, not on how hard the stimulus was.

why.correct: The rapid depolarization of an action potential depends on voltage-gated sodium channels. With them blocked, a depolarization can reach threshold values but no action potential follows, so no message travels to his brain.
options: Correct. No sodium channels, no action potential, so nothing carries the message along the fiber.
The resting potential is set by leak channels, which lidocaine does not block. It stays near −70 mV.
Graded potentials at the nerve endings come from other channels, such as mechanically gated ones, and still occur. They just cannot be turned into action potentials.
Refractoriness follows an action potential and lasts milliseconds. Here, the drug prevents action potentials altogether, and the effect wears off as the drug is cleared.

why.correct: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels leaves rest and graded potentials intact but abolishes action potentials, so nothing travels along the fiber.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: Rest is set by leak channels and the ion gradients, which the toxin does not touch.

variables.name: Graded potential at the nerve ending
variables.why: The stimulus still opens its own channels at the ending, so the graded potential is the same size.

variables.name: Number of action potentials along the fiber
variables.why: Without voltage-gated sodium channels, reaching threshold cannot start the self-reinforcing sodium entry, so no action potentials occur.

variables.name: Peak voltage reached along the fiber
variables.why: With no sodium rush, the membrane never swings to +30 mV; it only shows fading graded changes.

why.correct: Threshold opens the sodium channels; sodium entry drives the rise to about +30 mV; sodium channels then close as slow potassium channels let potassium out (repolarization); the slow-closing potassium channels cause a brief hyperpolarization before rest returns.

Repolarization comes from potassium flowing out through voltage-gated potassium channels, after the sodium channels close on their own. The pump is far too slow to do this, and so few ions move in one action potential that the pump need not act at once.
options: This is right: an action potential starts when the membrane reaches threshold.
This is right: sodium entry drives the rapid depolarization.
This is right: the peak is about +30 mV in a typical neuron.
This is the error. Potassium leaving through voltage-gated channels repolarizes the membrane; the pump only keeps the gradients steady over time.
This is right: extra potassium leaves while those channels close, so the membrane dips below rest.

why.correct: At threshold, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open that sodium entry outpaces potassium exit. The entering positive charge drives the rapid rise.
options: Potassium leaving would make the inside more negative. That drives repolarization, which comes after the peak.
Correct. Sodium rushing in drives the rapid rise toward sodium's equilibrium potential.
The pump moves more positive charge out than in, which would make the inside slightly more negative, and it is far too slow to shape an action potential.
Leak channels stay open throughout. The rise comes from voltage-gated sodium channels opening.

why.correct: The steep rise is sodium rushing in through voltage-gated sodium channels, down its electrochemical gradient, pulling the membrane toward sodium's equilibrium potential.
options: Potassium leaving makes the inside more negative. It produces the steep fall after the peak.
Chloride entering brings negative charge in, which would hyperpolarize the membrane.
Correct. Sodium entry drives the rising part of the action potential.
Pumping sodium out would make the inside more negative, and the pump is too slow to produce a change within a millisecond.

why.correct: The bumps grow with stimulus size, which is what graded means. An action potential starts only when a depolarization reaches the threshold line.
options: Correct. The bumps vary in size, which is what graded means, and threshold is the gate to an action potential.
The bumps come in several sizes, so they are not all-or-none. Only action potentials are.
Threshold lies above rest, so dips below rest move the membrane farther from it.
The wider bump on the graph lasts longer but stays below threshold. Duration alone does not start an action potential; reaching threshold does.

why.correct: Graded potentials add together. The hyperpolarization moved the membrane farther from threshold, so the same depolarization now falls short more often. Hyperpolarizing graded potentials make firing less likely.
options: Starting from a more negative value puts threshold farther away, not closer.
Correct. The membrane needs a bigger depolarization to reach threshold from −76 mV.
Graded potentials combine, so the earlier hyperpolarization changes the outcome.
Nothing makes firing certain regardless of stimulus size. Here the odds went down.

why.correct: Charge spreads both ways, but the patch behind has just fired: its sodium channels have closed on their own and cannot reopen yet. Only the patch ahead can reach threshold and fire.
options: Correct. The refractory period of the patch behind makes propagation one-way.
Voltage-gated sodium channels are spread along the axon. Their state, not their position, prevents backward firing.
Charge spreads both ways from the firing patch. The lab-dish example shows this: started in the middle, the action potential travels in both directions.
The terminals do not pull ions toward themselves. Propagation is driven by each patch firing in turn.

why.correct: Half a millisecond in, the membrane is in its refractory period. The sodium channels are either already open or have closed on their own and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so a new action potential cannot start.
options: The sodium channels are not available to start a new action potential during the refractory period.
Action potentials are all-or-none; an extra stimulus does not add to one in progress.
Correct. The refractory period blocks a second action potential this soon.
The stimulus is depolarizing, and the membrane is in the middle of an action potential. Nothing here causes an immediate hyperpolarization.

why.correct: Sodium channels still open and close on their own, so the rise is normal. But the fast exit of potassium that drives repolarization is gone; only the slower leak channels bring the membrane back, so repolarization takes longer.
options: Threshold and the rise depend on sodium channels, which work normally.
Sodium entry cannot drive the membrane past sodium's equilibrium potential, about +60 mV.
The dip below rest is caused by voltage-gated potassium channels that are slow to close. With them blocked, the dip is smaller, not deeper.
Correct. Without voltage-gated potassium channels, repolarization relies on leak channels and is slow.

why.correct: Each patch of axon regenerates a fresh, full-sized action potential as the one before it depolarizes it to threshold. Propagation is rebuilding at every patch, not passive spreading, so the size does not shrink with distance.
options: Graded potentials fade within a millimeter or two, but action potentials are rebuilt at every patch.
Rebuilding the action potential at each patch restores the full size, so there is no gradual loss.
The peak is set by the same channels at every patch, so it does not grow either.
Correct. An action potential arrives as large as it started.

why.correct: Charge spreads farther inside a wider axon before leaking out, so it brings patches farther ahead to threshold sooner. Wider axons conduct faster.
options: Correct. Greater diameter means faster propagation.
A narrow axon resists the spread of charge more, so each patch reaches threshold later. It is slower.
Diameter affects speed, so the two differ.
Unwrapped axons do propagate action potentials, just more slowly than wrapped ones of similar size.

why.correct: Voltage-gated sodium channels close on their own after opening and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes. A membrane held depolarized for a long time keeps many of them in that closed state, so fewer are available to produce an action potential, and the cells respond weakly or not at all.
options: High blood potassium makes the resting potential less negative, not more.
Correct. Sustained depolarization leaves too few sodium channels ready to open.
High outside potassium does not stop potassium channels from opening. The problem lies with the sodium channels.
Higher potassium outside does not block the pump. The weakness comes from the sodium channels, not the pump.

why.correct: Graded potentials can go in either direction, depending on which channels the stimulus opens. An action potential always starts as a depolarization; the brief hyperpolarization at its end follows the spike.
options: Correct. A graded potential can be a pure hyperpolarization. An action potential always starts with a depolarization, and its brief dip below rest comes only after the spike.
Action potentials depend on voltage-gated sodium channels. Graded potentials come from whatever channels the stimulus opens.
This describes an action potential. Graded potentials fade within a millimeter or two.
The refractory period follows an action potential. Graded potentials have none and can add together.

why.correct: A ligand (Latin ligare, to bind) is any molecule that binds specifically to a site on a protein. Chemical messengers, and drugs that bind the same proteins, are ligands.
options: A channel that is always open is a leak channel. A ligand is the molecule that binds, not the protein.
A cell that responds to a messenger is a target cell.
Some enzymes do break down messengers, but a ligand is the molecule that binds, not an enzyme acting on it.
Correct. Binding specifically to a protein is what makes a molecule a ligand.

why.correct: Only target cells respond to a messenger, and a target cell is one with receptor proteins that fit it. The skin and fat cells meet the hormone but have no receptor proteins for it.
options: The question says the hormone reaches all three tissues equally. Reaching a cell is not enough; the cell must have a matching receptor protein.
Energy supply does not decide which cells respond. Receptor proteins do.
Correct. Matching receptor proteins make the liver cells target cells.
Whether a messenger enters a cell depends on its solubility, not the tissue. The response still requires a matching receptor protein.

why.correct: The receptor protein, and the machinery it is linked to inside the cell, decides the response. Different receptor proteins for the same messenger can start different pathways in different cells.
options: A smaller amount would give a weaker version of the same response, not a different kind of response.
Correct. Different receptor proteins link the same messenger to different responses.
The same molecule acts in both places; the difference lies in the cells receiving it.
If heart cells had no receptor proteins for it, they would not respond to it at all. They do respond, through their own receptor proteins.

why.correct: Paracrine signaling (para- = beside) is a messenger acting on neighboring cells after diffusing a short distance. Nitric oxide from the endothelium acting on nearby smooth muscle is a classic example.
options: Autocrine signaling acts on the releasing cell itself. Here the endothelium signals a different, neighboring cell.
A hormone travels in the blood to distant targets. Nitric oxide acts only a few micrometers away and is gone within seconds.
Synaptic signaling is a neuron releasing neurotransmitter across a synapse. Endothelial cells are not neurons.
Correct. Short-distance diffusion to a neighbor is paracrine signaling.

why.correct: Autocrine signaling (auto- = self) is a messenger binding receptor proteins on the same cell that released it.
options: Paracrine signaling acts on neighboring cells. Here the releasing cell is also the target.
Correct. The cell signals itself.
The interleukin never travels in the blood to a distant target.
No neuron or synapse is involved.

why.correct: Ibuprofen blocks the enzyme that makes prostaglandins from a membrane fatty acid. Less prostaglandin means less sensitized pain nerve endings and less vessel dilation in the ankle, but also less protection for the stomach lining.
options: Ibuprofen does not act on neurotransmitter receptor proteins. Its effects come from reduced prostaglandin production.
Ibuprofen is not a general cAMP booster. A change in one local messenger, prostaglandins, explains both effects.
Correct. One enzyme block explains both the relief and the side effect.
Ibuprofen does not kill white blood cells. It reduces a local messenger.

why.correct: A small hydrophobic molecule dissolves through the phospholipid bilayer, so it can reach receptor proteins inside the cell. Steroids made from cholesterol bind intracellular receptors.
options: Correct. Lipid-soluble messengers cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors.
Membrane receptor proteins serve water-soluble messengers that cannot cross the bilayer.
Proteins in the plasma carry lipid-soluble messengers, but they are transport proteins, not the receptor proteins that start the response.
Intracellular receptors sit in the cytosol or inside the nucleus, not on the outer surface of the nuclear envelope.

why.correct: The inhaled drug binds a membrane receptor protein and raises cAMP, which changes proteins the muscle cell already has: seconds to minutes. The steroid crosses the membrane, binds an intracellular receptor and changes transcription, so the cell must make new proteins: hours to start, and the proteins persist.
options: Absorption takes some time, but even a steroid given into a vein takes hours to act, and slow absorption cannot explain an effect that outlasts the drug. The delay and the long effect come from making new proteins.
Correct. Changing existing proteins is fast; changing gene expression is slow and lasting.
Both drugs act on the same airways. The speed difference comes from where their receptor proteins are and what they change.
Concentration changes how strong a response is, not whether it takes minutes or hours to start.

why.correct: The signal passes from the first messenger outside, through the receptor protein and G protein in the membrane, to the enzyme making cAMP (the second messenger) inside, and then to phosphorylated proteins that carry out the response.
A water-soluble messenger cannot cross the hydrophobic core of the bilayer. It binds a receptor protein in the plasma membrane and passes its signal inward through a G protein and second messenger.
options: This is right: water-soluble messengers dissolve in the plasma.
This is the error. Crossing the membrane and binding a receptor protein in the nucleus describes a lipid-soluble messenger.
This is right: the occupied membrane receptor protein switches on a G protein.
This is right: the enzyme switched on by the G protein makes cAMP from ATP.
This is right: phosphorylation changes the activity of the target proteins.

why.correct: Calcium entry triggers vesicles full of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and empty into the cleft. The neurotransmitter then diffuses across and binds receptor proteins.
options: The electrical signal cannot cross the cleft; that is why a chemical messenger is needed.
The calcium that matters here enters the presynaptic axon terminal. The postsynaptic cell does not release it.
Correct. Calcium triggers exocytosis of neurotransmitter.
Neurotransmitter is made inside the presynaptic cell and stored in vesicles, not made in the cleft.

why.correct: Blocking cAMP breakdown leaves the first messenger's binding unchanged but raises cAMP, strengthening and prolonging everything downstream.

variables.name: Number of receptor proteins occupied by the messenger
variables.why: The drug acts inside the cell, after the receptor protein; it does not change how much messenger binds.

variables.name: cAMP concentration inside the cells
variables.why: cAMP is still made at the usual rate but broken down more slowly, so it builds up.

variables.name: Phosphorylation of the target proteins
variables.why: More cAMP switches on more of the enzymes that phosphorylate target proteins.

variables.name: How long the response lasts after the messenger leaves
variables.why: Breaking down cAMP is what ends the response; slowing that step lets the response continue longer.

why.correct: One occupied receptor protein switches on many G proteins, each switched-on enzyme makes many cAMP molecules, and each enzyme cAMP switches on modifies many proteins. This signal amplification turns a few messenger molecules into a large response.
options: One messenger molecule binds one receptor protein at a time. The multiplying happens inside the cell.
Correct. Amplification at each step explains the large response.
Hormones are not fuel. They carry information by binding receptor proteins; they do not become ATP.
Target cells do not need to concentrate the hormone. The pathway downstream of the receptor protein does the multiplying.

why.correct: When a messenger or drug stays high for a long time, target cells reduce their receptor proteins, often by endocytosis and breakdown. With fewer receptor proteins, the same dose produces a smaller response.
options: Up-regulation would add receptor proteins and make the response stronger, not weaker.
Membrane receptor proteins are not moved into the nucleus. Down-regulated receptor proteins are taken in and broken down.
Correct. Fewer receptor proteins, weaker response to the same dose.
Nothing here points to an energy failure. The same dose working less points to fewer receptor proteins.

why.correct: When a messenger stays low for a long time, target cells add receptor proteins. Without the nerve's neurotransmitter, the fibers insert its receptor proteins across their whole surface and become far more sensitive.
options: Correct. Long-term absence of a messenger leads to up-regulation.
Down-regulation would reduce receptor proteins and weaken the response. The response became stronger.
Solubility is a property of the molecule and does not change. The change is in the target cells.
Autocrine signaling means a cell responding to its own messenger. The fibers are responding to a neurotransmitter applied from outside.

why.correct: Lipid-soluble messengers cross the bilayer, bind receptor proteins inside the cell, and change transcription. Being hydrophobic, they ride in the blood bound to carrier proteins. Making new proteins takes hours, so they are slow.
options: True. Their hydrophobic structure lets them dissolve through the bilayer.
True. Their receptor proteins are in the cytosol or nucleus.
True. The messenger–receptor pair acts as a transcription factor.
False. Changing gene expression takes hours. Millisecond responses belong to neurotransmitters acting on ion channels.
True. Hydrophobic molecules dissolve poorly in plasma, so most are carried bound to proteins.

why.correct: Nervous signaling sends action potentials along axons and releases neurotransmitter across synapses onto specific muscle fibers within milliseconds. A hormone must travel through the blood and reaches every target cell, so it is too slow and too widespread for a precise, split-second action.
options: Blood reaches the arm, so hormones can too. The problem is speed and precision.
Many hormones act on muscle. The issue is the time a hormone takes to arrive and act.
Neurotransmitters are not carried in the blood to reach muscles; they cross the synaptic cleft at each synapse.
Correct. Fast, precise responses are the strength of nervous signaling.

why.correct: The G protein links the receptor protein to the enzyme that makes cAMP. With that link broken, binding at the surface produces no second messenger, so the signal stops at the membrane.
options: cAMP is made only after the G protein switches on the membrane enzyme, which cannot happen here.
The receptor protein does not make cAMP; a separate membrane enzyme does, once a G protein switches it on.
A water-soluble messenger cannot cross the membrane, whatever happens to the G protein.
Correct. Without the G protein, the signal cannot pass from the receptor protein to the cAMP-making enzyme.

why.correct: Everything on the presynaptic side works: the action potential arrives, calcium enters and neurotransmitter is released. But with its receptor proteins blocked, the neurotransmitter cannot open the postsynaptic channels, so the postsynaptic cell barely responds.
options: Correct. Release is normal; the block is at the receptor proteins.
Release depends on the presynaptic side, which the drug does not affect.
Blocking receptor proteins reduces the postsynaptic response; it does not increase firing.
The drug acts on the postsynaptic membrane. The presynaptic action potential travels normally.

why.correct: A receptor protein is a molecule that binds a messenger and changes shape to start a response. A sensory receptor is a cell or nerve ending that detects a change in the body or its surroundings.
options: This detects a physical change, so it is a sensory receptor.
This detects light, so it is a sensory receptor.
Correct. Binding a chemical messenger is what a receptor protein does.
This detects temperature, so it is a sensory receptor.

why.correct: Exocrine means secreting outward. The defining feature is the route: the product enters a duct (or, for a one-cell gland, lands directly on a surface) and acts on that surface.
options: Many exocrine glands do release enzymes, but some release mucus or watery fluid instead. Glands are classified by where the product goes, not by what it is.
Correct. A duct that carries the product to a surface, such as the skin or the inside of the gut, is what makes a gland exocrine.
Glands of both kinds are built from epithelium, not connective tissue. A patch of epithelium grows down into the connective tissue beneath it and becomes the gland.
A dense capillary network is typical of endocrine glands, whose hormones must enter the blood. It does not define an exocrine gland.

why.correct: No duct plus a rich capillary supply is the signature of an endocrine gland. Its cells release hormones into the interstitial fluid, and the hormones diffuse into the nearby capillaries.
options: A simple tubular gland is exocrine, so it has a duct running to a surface. The absence of any duct rules it out.
A mucous gland is a kind of exocrine gland. It releases mucus through a duct onto a surface, and no duct is present here.
Correct. Ductless cells surrounded by capillaries release their product toward the blood: that is an endocrine gland.
A unicellular exocrine gland, such as a goblet cell, is a single cell sitting in a surface lining. This is a cluster of cells with no surface to empty onto.

why.correct: The pancreas holds two kinds of gland. Its enzyme-making cells are exocrine and drain through the duct, so a blocked duct stops enzymes reaching the gut and fat goes undigested. Its hormone clusters are endocrine: they release into interstitial fluid and capillaries, so a blocked duct does not affect them.
options: If the hormone-making cells were destroyed, hormone levels would fall. They stayed normal.
If both products shared the duct, blocking it would lower both. Normal hormone levels show the hormones take a different route.
Nothing in the case suggests the tumor makes hormones, and it would not explain the undigested fat. The simpler explanation is that the two products take different routes.
Correct. Blocking the duct stops the exocrine product (enzymes) but not the endocrine product (hormones), which never used the duct.

why.correct: A goblet cell is a gland made of one cell. It sits in the surface epithelium and releases mucus onto that surface, so it needs no duct and still counts as exocrine.
options: Correct. One cell, releasing its product onto a surface: a unicellular exocrine gland.
An endocrine gland releases hormones toward the blood. A goblet cell releases mucus onto a surface, which is exocrine.
A compound gland is multicellular with a branching duct. A goblet cell is a single cell with no duct.
A holocrine cell breaks apart to release its product. A goblet cell releases mucus by exocytosis and survives to make more.

why.correct: Name the duct first, then the secretory part. A branching duct makes the gland compound, and rounded sacs make it alveolar (also called acinar).
options: Simple means one unbranched duct, and tubular means tube-shaped secretory parts. This gland has neither feature.
The sacs fit alveolar, but simple means an unbranched duct. This duct branches repeatedly.
Correct. A branching duct (compound) that ends in rounded sacs (alveolar) is a compound alveolar gland.
The branching duct fits compound, but a tubuloalveolar gland has both tube-shaped and sac-shaped secretory parts. Every branch here ends in a rounded sac.

why.correct: In holocrine secretion the whole cell becomes the product. Cells fill with product, break apart, and are replaced by new cells from dividing stem cells at the base.
options: In merocrine secretion the cell releases vesicle contents by exocytosis and stays whole. Here the cells break apart.
Correct. Whole cells breaking apart and joining the secretion, with dividing cells at the base replacing them, is holocrine secretion.
In apocrine secretion only the apical part of the cell pinches off, and the rest of the cell survives. Here whole cells break apart.
Endocrine describes where a product goes (into the blood), not how a cell releases it. It is not a mode of secretion.

variables.name: Number of new secretory cells produced in the gland
variables.why: New holocrine cells come from stem cells dividing by mitosis. Stopping mitosis stops that supply.

variables.name: Amount of secretion the gland releases
variables.why: Each holocrine cell is used up when it breaks apart. With no new cells replacing them, fewer cells are left to fill and break apart, so output falls.

variables.name: Output of a nearby merocrine gland whose cells are not dividing
variables.why: A merocrine cell releases its product by exocytosis and survives, so it does not depend on a steady supply of new cells. Its output is unaffected.

why.correct: Endocrine glands are ductless. They release hormones into the interstitial fluid, the hormones diffuse into capillaries, and they act on target cells that carry the matching receptor protein.
options: True. Endocrine glands are also called ductless glands.
True. The hormone leaves the cell into interstitial fluid and diffuses into nearby capillaries.
True. A hormone reaches every tissue in the blood but changes only its target cells, the ones with a matching receptor protein.
False. Delivery through a duct to a surface such as the inside of the gut is what exocrine glands do.
False. Endocrine glands such as the thyroid gland are made of many cells. The one-cell gland you know, the goblet cell, is exocrine.

why.correct: This is the secretory pathway followed by merocrine release: build the protein on the rough ER, pack it in the Golgi, move vesicles to the apical side, fuse by exocytosis, and let the duct carry the product to its surface.
An endocrine gland has no duct. Its hormone first enters the interstitial fluid around the cell, then diffuses into a nearby capillary.
options: Correct. Between leaving the cell and entering a capillary, the hormone crosses the interstitial fluid by diffusion.
The pituitary gland is endocrine, so it has no duct. Ducts belong to exocrine glands.
Release onto a surface is what an exocrine gland does. An endocrine product heads for the blood.
A cell responding to its own product is autocrine signaling. That would not lead on to the hormone entering a capillary and traveling in the blood.

why.correct: An exocrine product stays in the duct system and is delivered to a surface. Entering capillaries is the route of an endocrine product.
options: This step is correct. The secretory portion of an alveolar gland is its rounded sacs.
This step is correct. Exocytosis on the apical side empties the product into the lumen of the sac.
This is the wrong step. An exocrine product does not enter the blood; it flows from the sac into the duct system.
This step is correct. In a compound gland, the branching ducts join like tree branches into one main duct.
This step is correct. The duct delivers the product to a surface, here the inside of the gut.

why.correct: Exocrine and endocrine describe the route, not the chemical. A duct to a surface means exocrine; release into interstitial fluid and then blood means endocrine. The student's rule fails whenever a product breaks the pattern, and it cannot classify mucus at all.
options: Enzymes are proteins, and so are many hormones. Knowing the product is a protein does not tell you which way it leaves.
Both exocrine and endocrine cells can store their product in secretory vesicles and release it by exocytosis.
Correct. Tracing where the product goes is the test that defines the two kinds of gland.
Size separates a goblet cell from larger exocrine glands, but it does not separate exocrine from endocrine: both kinds include many-celled glands.

why.correct: A serous gland (ser/o = watery fluid) releases a thin, watery fluid that is often rich in enzymes. Its cells hold many protein-filled vesicles.
options: A mucous gland releases thick, sticky mucus, made thick by large glycoproteins called mucins. This fluid is thin and watery.
Correct. Thin, watery, enzyme-rich fluid from protein-packed cells marks a serous gland.
Holocrine names how a cell releases its product (by breaking apart), not what the product is. Nothing here says the cells break apart.
A ductless gland is an endocrine gland. The question describes an exocrine gland.

why.correct: In the milk-making gland of the breast, fat droplets leave from the apical end of the cell wrapped in a piece of its plasma membrane: true apocrine release. Some exams instead name the "apocrine" sweat-producing glands of the armpit, but electron microscope studies show those release mainly by exocytosis, so their name is historical.
options: A goblet cell releases mucus by exocytosis and stays whole. That is merocrine secretion.
The oil glands of the skin are holocrine: whole cells fill with product and break apart.
The thyroid gland is endocrine. The three mode names describe exocrine glands, and its hormone release is not apocrine.
Correct. Fat droplets pinching off in a wrap of plasma membrane is the clearest example of apocrine release.

why.correct: Merocrine release is exocytosis. Vesicles empty their contents, and the cell loses nothing else, so it keeps working.
options: Correct. A merocrine cell releases only the vesicle contents and survives unchanged.
Losing the apical part of the cell with the product is apocrine secretion.
Breaking apart so the whole cell becomes the product is holocrine secretion.
A merocrine cell survives, so there is nothing to replace. Steady replacement by dividing stem cells is what holocrine glands need.

why.correct: An endocrine product enters the blood and can act far away. A chemical that diffuses only to nearby cells and acts on them is a paracrine signal. Lacking a duct does not by itself make cells an endocrine gland; the product must also reach the blood.
options: Endocrine signaling needs the messenger to enter the blood. This chemical never does, so the cells are not acting as an endocrine gland.
Correct. Local diffusion to neighboring cells without entering the blood is paracrine signaling.
Exocrine secretion delivers a product through a duct onto a surface. This chemical acts on neighboring cells inside the tissue.
Holocrine describes a cell breaking apart to release its product. Nothing here says the cells break apart, and the question is about where the chemical acts.

why.correct: Apo- means off or away. In apocrine secretion the apical end of the cell, holding the product, pinches off inside a wrap of plasma membrane, and the rest of the cell repairs itself.
options: Vesicle fusion with the cell left whole is merocrine secretion.
Correct. Losing the product-filled apical part of the cell is apocrine secretion.
A whole cell breaking apart is holocrine secretion.
Diffusion into capillaries describes the route of an endocrine product, not a mode of secretion.

why.correct: The synovial membrane is a connective tissue membrane. It is areolar connective tissue with a lining layer of cells facing the joint space, but no epithelium.
options: A mucous membrane is an epithelial membrane: an epithelium over the lamina propria.
A serous membrane is an epithelial membrane: simple squamous mesothelium over thin connective tissue.
Correct. The synovial membrane is the one connective tissue membrane.
The cutaneous membrane (skin) has an epithelium: the keratinized stratified squamous epidermis.

why.correct: A lining of a tract open to the outside, with epithelium over a lamina propria of loose connective tissue, is a mucous membrane (mucosa). The goblet cells keep it coated with mucus.
options: A serous membrane lines a closed cavity and has simple squamous epithelium, not columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, whose surface is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
A synovial membrane has no epithelium and lines the space inside a movable joint.
Correct. Epithelium plus lamina propria, lining a tube open to the outside, is a mucosa.

why.correct: The outer covering of the stomach is the visceral peritoneum, a serous membrane. Its simple squamous mesothelium releases thin serous fluid into the closed peritoneal cavity, which lets organs slide with little friction.
options: The stomach's inner lining is a mucous membrane, but this sample is from its outer surface, facing the closed abdominal cavity.
Correct. A single layer of flat cells lining a closed cavity is a serous membrane, and it releases serous fluid.
Synovial membranes line the spaces inside movable joints, not the abdominal cavity.
A mucous membrane lines a tract open to the outside and is not simple squamous. This membrane faces a closed cavity.

why.correct: An epithelial membrane is an epithelium attached to connective tissue. The mucous, serous and cutaneous membranes all fit.
options: Epithelial membrane: epithelium over the lamina propria.
Epithelial membrane: mesothelium over thin connective tissue.
Epithelial membrane: the epidermis over the dermis.
Not an epithelial membrane. The synovial membrane is made of connective tissue alone.
Not a tissue membrane at all. A plasma membrane is the lipid bilayer around a single cell.

why.correct: Histamine opens gaps between the endothelial cells of capillaries and the smallest veins. Water and proteins from plasma leak into the interstitial fluid, and the tissue swells.
options: Inflammation causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. Narrower arteries would bring less blood and would not cause swelling.
Collagen is laid down days later during repair. It does not explain swelling within an hour.
Correct. Fluid leaking out of leaky vessels into the interstitial fluid is what makes the tissue swell.
Mast cells release histamine within minutes; they do not multiply to cause swelling. The swelling comes from fluid, not extra cells.

variables.name: Amount of histamine released by mast cells
variables.why: The drug acts on the receptor proteins of the target cells, not on the mast cells, so release is unchanged.

variables.name: Blood flow into the area
variables.why: With its receptor proteins blocked, histamine causes less vasodilation of the small arteries, so less blood flows in and the area is less red and warm.

variables.name: Swelling
variables.why: Histamine can no longer make capillaries and the smallest veins as leaky, so less fluid leaks into the interstitial fluid.

why.correct: Bleeding and clotting come first. Chemical messengers then start inflammation, whose vessel changes bring in white blood cells. Macrophages clear the debris, which lets new capillaries and fibroblasts move in. The final outcome is regeneration where cells can divide and the framework survives, and fibrosis where it does not.

Cardiac muscle regenerates very little because its cells rarely divide. Fibroblasts filled the gap with collagen (fibrosis). Scar tissue holds the wall together but cannot contract, so that region stays still.
options: Correct. The muscle cells of the heart rarely divide, so the heart repairs by fibrosis, and scar tissue does not contract.
Cardiac muscle regenerates very little. Months later, the region is scar, not immature muscle.
Inflammation after an injury like this settles within weeks. A thin, still wall months later reflects scar tissue.
Cells that die from lost blood supply die by necrosis, not apoptosis, and the gap they leave is filled by repair.

why.correct: Regeneration needs cells of the lost type that can divide. Mature liver cells can re-enter the cell cycle and multiply; the heart's muscle cells rarely do, so the heart fills the gap with scar tissue.
options: Correct. Whether the working cells can divide is the main factor that decides regeneration or fibrosis.
The heart has a very rich blood supply too. Blood supply alone does not decide whether a tissue regenerates.
The heart does have fibroblasts; they are what make the scar. Having fibroblasts favors fibrosis, not regeneration.
Liver injury does cause inflammation. Inflammation starts repair in both organs; the outcome differs because of cell division.

why.correct: Swelling, membrane rupture, many neighboring cells dying together, and inflammation around them are the marks of necrosis, cell death caused by injury.
options: In apoptosis the cell shrinks and breaks into sealed pieces, and no inflammation follows.
Mitosis is cell division, not cell death.
Regeneration replaces lost cells; it is not a way cells die.
Correct. Swollen, ruptured cells with inflammation around them point to necrosis.

why.correct: In apoptosis the cell breaks into small membrane-wrapped pieces, and macrophages engulf them before anything spills. In necrosis the membrane ruptures and the spilled contents act as danger signals that start inflammation.
options: Histamine comes mainly from mast cells, and extra histamine would promote inflammation, not prevent it.
Apoptosis happens throughout the body, including in tissues with a rich blood supply, such as the gut lining.
Correct. The apoptotic cell breaks into membrane-wrapped pieces that macrophages engulf before anything spills, so there are no danger signals to start inflammation.
This describes apoptosis, not necrosis. Necrotic cells swell and burst.

why.correct: Histamine causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. Wider small arteries bring in more warm blood, which is why an inflamed area is red and warm.
options: This step is correct. Mast cells hold histamine in granules and release it when tissue is injured.
This is the wrong step. Vasoconstriction would reduce blood flow and make the area pale and cool, the opposite of what you see.
This step is correct. That leakiness is what lets fluid and proteins from the plasma out of the vessels.
This step is correct. Fluid leaking into the interstitial fluid causes the swelling.
This step is correct. That is where the pain of inflammation comes from.

why.correct: Histamine causes vasodilation of the small arteries that feed the injured area. Wider vessels carry more warm blood in, causing redness and heat.
options: Correct. Vasodilation is the step between histamine release and increased blood flow.
Collagen deposition is a later repair step and does not change blood flow.
Clotted capillaries would reduce blood flow, not increase it.
Macrophages clear debris, but that does not explain the increased blood flow.

why.correct: Epidermis regenerates well, but it needs an intact framework to rebuild the right shape. In a shallow scrape the deeper connective tissue survives, so stem cells regrow normal skin. In a deep cut the framework is destroyed and collagen fills the gap as scar tissue.
options: A bigger clot does not make regeneration more likely. The deep cut destroys the framework, so it is the one that scars.
Correct. Surviving framework plus dividing stem cells in the epidermis allows regeneration without a scar.
Both involve skin, but depth decides the outcome. The deep cut loses its framework and scars.
Shallow injuries of the epidermis regenerate without scarring. Fibrosis fills only deeper gaps.

why.correct: The parenchyma is the organ's working cells, the ones that do its job. Regeneration replaces parenchyma with parenchyma; fibrosis replaces it with connective tissue.
options: The connective tissue framework supports the parenchyma and carries its blood vessels, but it is not the parenchyma.
A serous covering is a membrane on the outside of some organs, not their working cells.
Correct. The parenchyma is the functional cells of an organ.
Scar tissue replaces lost parenchyma; it is not parenchyma.

why.correct: The space inside a movable joint such as the knee is lined by a synovial membrane. It is a connective tissue membrane, and its lining cells release the thick, slippery joint fluid.
options: Serous membranes line the closed body cavities, such as the pleural and peritoneal cavities, not joint spaces.
Mucous membranes line tracts open to the outside of the body. The space inside the knee is sealed.
Correct. A synovial membrane, made of connective tissue, lines the joint and releases its fluid.
The skin covers the knee from outside. It does not line the joint space or release joint fluid.

why.correct: The cutaneous membrane is the only dry membrane. Its outer cells are dead and filled with keratin, and it releases no mucus or serous fluid onto its surface.
options: Correct. A dry, keratinized surface is what sets the skin apart.
All three epithelial membranes rest on connective tissue, so this does not set the skin apart.
Every tissue membrane covers or lines something, so this does not distinguish the skin.
The mucosa of the mouth is also stratified, so having several cell layers is not unique to the skin.

variables.name: Amount of collagen in the liver
variables.why: With each round of injury, fibroblasts lay down more collagen, and fibrosis builds up faster than it is removed.

variables.name: Number of working liver cells (parenchyma)
variables.why: Scar tissue gradually replaces working cells, and the scar distorts the framework that regeneration needs.

variables.name: The liver's ability to do its jobs
variables.why: Scar tissue holds the organ together but does not do the work of the lost liver cells, so function falls as the scar grows.

why.correct: The set point is the target value, such as about 37 °C for body temperature. It sits inside the normal range, and negative feedback pulls the variable back toward it.
options: The top of the normal range is not the set point. The set point sits inside the range, and the variable swings above and below it.
Correct. The set point is the value the control center compares the input with.
A positive feedback loop ends with an outside event, such as delivery of a baby. That is not what a set point means.
A set point is a value, not a location. Sensory receptors detect the variable; the control center compares it with the set point.

why.correct: After the stimulus changes the regulated variable, the sensory receptor (sensor) detects it and sends information along the afferent pathway (toward) to the control center. The control center compares it with the set point and sends commands along the efferent pathway (away) to the effector, which produces the response.
The effector is the tissue that carries out the command. Here the smooth muscle in the vessel walls contracts, causing vasoconstriction.
options: The cold air causes the stimulus, the drop in temperature. It is not part of the body's loop.
Nerves carrying commands from the brain are the efferent pathway, not the effector.
Correct. The smooth muscle does the work that changes the variable, so it is the effector.
The brain region that compares temperature with the set point is the control center.

why.correct: The afferent pathway (af- = toward) carries information from the sensory receptor toward the control center. Sensory nerves running from the skin to the brain do exactly that.
options: The efferent pathway carries commands away from the control center to the effector. These nerves carry information toward it.
The control center is where input is compared with the set point: here, a region of the brain. The nerves only carry the information there.
Correct. Signals arriving at the control center travel on the afferent pathway.
An effector carries out a response. These nerves do not change body temperature themselves.

variables.name: Diameter of the blood vessels in your skin
variables.why: The control center sends signals that relax the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels, so they dilate (vasodilation).

variables.name: Amount of sweat released onto your skin
variables.why: The control center signals the sweat glands to release sweat; as it evaporates, it carries heat away.

variables.name: Heat lost from your skin to the air
variables.why: More warm blood near the surface and more evaporating sweat both increase heat loss, which opposes the rise in temperature.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
variables.why: With the efferent pathway to the vessels broken, the command to constrict never arrives, so the skin vessels stay wider than in an intact person.

variables.name: Heat lost through the skin
variables.why: More warm blood near the cold surface loses more heat to the air.

variables.name: Body temperature after an hour
variables.why: Heat loss is not reduced, so body temperature falls further below the set point than it would in a person with an intact loop.

why.correct: Each response (more platelets sticking) strengthens the stimulus that caused it (more of the chemicals). A response that amplifies its own stimulus is positive feedback. The loop ends only when the tear is sealed.
options: Correct. The response strengthens the stimulus, so the change grows until an outside event, sealing the tear, stops it.
Negative feedback would oppose the change and reduce platelet sticking. Here each step increases it.
Mass balance compares inputs and outputs of a substance. It does not describe a loop in which a response amplifies itself.
Feedforward control starts a response before a variable changes. Here the response follows and strengthens an existing change.

why.correct: Labor contractions are driven by positive feedback: stretch of the lower opening of the uterus causes hormone release, which strengthens contractions, which cause more stretch. A positive loop cannot stop itself. Delivery is an outside event that removes the stretch, so the stimulus disappears and the loop ends.
options: The contractions grew stronger, not steadier, which is positive feedback. There is no set point that they are returned to.
Muscle does not simply run out of ATP within minutes of delivery. The loop stops because its stimulus is gone.
Correct. Removing the stretch removes the stimulus, and a positive loop ends when its stimulus is removed from outside.
Positive feedback does not settle at a set point. The loop ends because something outside it, delivery, removes the stimulus.

why.correct: "Negative" means the response opposes the stimulus, not that it lowers the variable. The stimulus was a fall in pH; the response raises it. Opposing the change back toward the set point is negative feedback.
options: Positive feedback would push the pH further in the direction it was already moving, lower still. Here the response raises it, which opposes the change.
Correct. A fall triggered a rise: the response opposes the change, which is negative feedback. "Negative" means opposing, not lowering.
Mass balance compares the input and output of a substance. It describes what disturbs a variable, not the loop that corrects it.
A response that pulls the variable back toward its set point is a feedback loop at work. Moving outside the normal range is the stimulus that starts it.

why.correct: Negative feedback opposes the change. That pulls the variable back toward the set point, whichever direction it moved, and the loop switches itself off as the stimulus shrinks.
options: True. Opposing the stimulus is the defining feature of negative feedback.
True. Opposing the change returns the variable toward its set point.
True. If the variable falls, the opposing response raises it, as when shivering warms a cold body.
False. Needing an outside event to stop is a feature of positive feedback. Negative feedback stops itself as the stimulus shrinks.
False. A response that enlarges the original change is positive feedback.

why.correct: Mass balance: change = input − output = 2.8 L − 2.4 L = +0.4 L per day. With input greater than output every day, body water builds up.
options: The amount stays the same only if input equals output. Here input is larger by 0.4 liters a day.
Body water falls only when output exceeds input. Here output is smaller.
Correct. Input exceeds output, so water accumulates, about 0.4 liters a day.
Nothing in the numbers changes during the week. As long as input exceeds output, water keeps accumulating.

why.correct: Change per day = input − output = 200 − 170 = +30 mmol. Over four days: 30 × 4 = +120 mmol.
options: The sign is wrong. Input is larger than output, so sodium builds up rather than falling.
30 mmol is the change for one day. Multiply by four days.
Correct. +30 mmol per day for four days is +120 mmol.
800 mmol is the total input over four days. The change in the body is input minus output.

why.correct: To lose heat, the skin's blood vessels dilate, bringing warm blood to the surface. Constriction would keep warm blood away from the skin and reduce heat loss, which is the response to cold.
options: This step is correct. A rise in temperature is the stimulus.
This step is correct. These nerve endings are the sensory receptors.
This step is correct. This is the afferent pathway to the control center.
This is the wrong step. A rise in temperature calls for vasodilation of skin vessels, not vasoconstriction.
This step is correct, but only if the vessels dilate. It is the response that opposes the stimulus.

why.correct: Information travels from the sensory receptor toward the control center along the afferent pathway (af- = toward).
options: The set point is the value the control center compares against. It is not a step the signal travels along.
Correct. The afferent pathway links the sensory receptor to the control center.
The regulated variable is what the stimulus changes and the response corrects. It is not a pathway.
A target cell is a cell with a receptor protein for a messenger. It is not a slot in the loop.

why.correct: Her sensors, pathways and control center work, so the command to lose heat is sent. Her effectors, the skin blood vessels and the sweat glands, respond weakly, and the heat load of the heat wave is larger than they can oppose. That is a homeostatic imbalance caused by overwhelmed effectors.
options: Her nerves and control center work normally, and her body is responding to the heat, so detection is intact.
The case says her nerves work normally. Signals are reaching the control center.
The control center works normally and is sending commands. The problem is how strongly the effectors carry them out.
Correct. Weak vasodilation and little sweat mean the effectors cannot match the heat load.

variables.name: Skin temperature in the first minute
variables.why: Cold air draws heat from your skin at once, before any loop has had time to respond. This fall is the stimulus.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin after the loop has responded
variables.why: The control center signals the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels to contract, and vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the surface.

variables.name: Heat produced by skeletal muscles after the loop has responded
variables.why: Skeletal muscles, acting as effectors, contract in rapid small bursts (shivering), and those contractions release heat.

variables.name: Body temperature after an hour
variables.why: Reduced heat loss and increased heat production oppose the cooling, so negative feedback holds body temperature close to its set point, near where it started.

variables.name: Signals from the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors
variables.why: Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors fire fewer action potentials; the control center reads this as a fall.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The control center sends signals along the efferent pathway that speed up the heart, which pumps more blood per minute and raises pressure.

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries
variables.why: The control center triggers vasoconstriction of small arteries. Narrower vessels raise resistance, which raises pressure back toward the set point.

why.correct: The control center (integrating center) receives the input, compares it with the set point, and sends commands along the efferent pathway.
options: Detecting the change is the job of the sensory receptor (sensor).
Carrying out the response is the job of the effector.
Correct. The control center compares the input with the set point and sends commands along the efferent pathway.
Carrying signals toward the control center is the job of the afferent pathway.

why.correct: Detecting a change, sending signals and getting effectors working all take time. By the time the response takes hold, the variable has moved, so the correction carries it slightly past the set point, and the loop then corrects the other way. The result is small swings within the normal range.
options: Correct. The time lag in a negative feedback loop means each correction carries the variable slightly past the set point, producing small oscillations.
Positive feedback would push temperature further away, not back. The small swings come from negative feedback.
The set point shifts slowly over the day, not randomly minute to minute, and that would not explain swings around it.
Sensory receptors keep reporting the variable; that is how the loop detects the next swing. Switching off is not the cause.

why.correct: Higher temperature causes more heat release, which raises temperature further: the response strengthens the stimulus. When negative feedback has failed, this harmful positive feedback loop can drive temperature up until cells are damaged, so outside cooling is needed.
options: Negative feedback has already failed to hold the temperature; the danger is that it is being overwhelmed, not that it overcorrects.
Correct. More heat causes more heat: a positive feedback loop that needs outside intervention to stop.
A set point does not fall to match a rising temperature. The problem is that the variable is being driven away from the set point.
Mass balance describes what happens when input and output differ; it does not force them to match. Here heat input exceeds output, so heat builds up.

why.correct: The efferent pathway carries the command from the control center to the effector. Here the command is a hormone carried in the blood from the kidneys to the bone marrow. An efferent pathway can be a hormone as well as a nerve.
options: The kidney cells that detect low oxygen act as the sensory receptor and the control center; they are not the pathway.
Correct. The hormone carries the command to the effector, so it is the efferent pathway.
More red blood cells carrying more oxygen is the response, not the pathway.
The bone marrow carries out the command, so it is the effector.

why.correct: In labor, stronger contractions cause more stretch, which causes more hormone release and stronger contractions still. The response strengthens the stimulus, which is positive feedback.
options: Body temperature is held near its set point by negative feedback: cold triggers responses that warm you.
Blood pressure is held by negative feedback: a fall triggers responses that raise it.
Blood pH is held by negative feedback: a fall triggers responses that raise it back toward 7.40.
Correct. Labor contractions build on themselves until delivery ends the loop.
